Two deliberately NOT scaled: BETWEEN_PITCH_MS (measured/conformed) and UMP_CALL_DELAY_MS (carries a 150-250ms partialReading -- scaling moves it away from the measurement).

swingWindows.what: The swing timing windows, and why they can never be measured from BB footage.
swingWindows.finding: A timing window is an INTERNAL TOLERANCE -- how many ms of error still makes contact -- with no on-screen representation. No amount of video reveals BB's, because you would need the player's exact tap times, which no recording captures. So unlike the flight time, this constant has to be CHOSEN.
swingWindows.whatForcedIt: Matching BB's 270ms fastball made the old windows structurally broken, not merely mistuned: CONTACT was 380ms, wider than the entire flight, so an errorMs of -270 (a tap at the instant of release) sat inside the band and contact was guaranteed. Verified against the real code path -- bandFromError compares Math.abs(errorMs) to absolute-ms constants and never references travelMs.
swingWindows.choice: Scaled by exactly the factor the flight scaled (0.371), so every internal relationship is unchanged: window as a fraction of flight, and the SWING_TYPES deltas relative to the windows. main 120/240/380 -> 45/89/141; kid 80/170/300 -> 30/63/111; SWING_TYPES SAFE 60->22, BIG 45->17, BUNT 80->30, CRAZY_BUNT 100->37.
swingWindows.caveat: This preserves the RATIO, not the absolute difficulty. Human timing jitter is absolute (~50-100ms), so a 30ms PERFECT band is genuinely harder to hit than an 80ms one -- batting IS harder now, and a 270ms flight rewards anticipation over reaction, which is what BB does too. These are the first dial to widen if it plays badly. TEE_PITCH_MS (1500, untouched) is the escape hatch for the youngest players.
swingWindows.structuralInvariant: CONTACT must stay below the FASTEST possible travelMs in every mode, or timing becomes free again. Asserted in conformance.test.js.

pitchWindup.what: How long BB2001's pitcher takes from his first delivery motion to releasing the ball.
pitchWindup.whyThisRecordExists: Nothing had ever measured it, and it turned out to be half the problem. Our ANIM.WINDUP_MS was 380ms against BB's ~770ms, so the ball arrived with barely any telegraph -- which reads as 'too fast' even independently of the flight itself.

partialReading.bracket: delivery motion begins ~12:58.10, release 12:58.87 (same stopwatch-gated pitch as pace.pitchCorridor)
partialReading.note: From the SET position (12:57.57) it is ~1.3s. The 770ms figure counts only from the first delivery motion, which is the batter-visible telegraph.
partialReading.why: n=1; needs n>=3 like the corridor.

ours.snapshot: 380 -> 800 on 2026-07-26. The two existing windup frames now hold ~400ms each; if that reads stiff the fix is more poses, not a shorter windup.

pitchWindup.whatWouldWork: Bracket the delivery start on n>=3 pitches from the stopwatch-gated capture.

simClock.what: Why every pace.* record is allowed to be an absolute real-millisecond claim, and what would silently make them all wrong.
simClock.theClaim: GameScene steps the live sim on Phaser's raw frame delta, so one sim-millisecond IS one real-millisecond. That is the only reason a constant in config.ts can be compared against a stopwatch reading off BB2001 -- pace.homeToFirst's 4197ms, pace.flyHang's 2875-5075, all of it.
simClock.theTrap: conformance.test.js's ourHomeToFirstMs passes `tempo: 1` as a LITERAL, and was commented as though that defended the claim: 'introducing a tempo dial later breaks HERE, loudly, instead of silently invalidating every ratio in measures.json'. It does not. A tempo scalar changes what the game DOES and changes nothing the test COMPUTES.
simClock.theEvidence: PR #17 (Split action tempo into TEMPO and PITCH_TEMPO, opened 2026-07-23, closed 2026-07-28) was test-merged into main on 2026-07-28. With TEMPO 0.6 the real home->1B becomes 6995ms against BB's measured 4200 -- 66% too slow -- while pace.homeToFirst went on reporting 4197 and conformed. Fly hang became 4792-8458 real. All 449 tests passed.
simClock.whyItWasTemptingAndWrong: PR #17's premise was correct when written: home->1B ran ~2.1s. The 2026-07-24 pace retune fixed that at the source by moving LIVE.RUNNER_SPEED to 42.8 px/s. A tempo scalar landing afterwards applies the same correction a second time.
simClock.theGuard: scripts/simclock.lint.test.js. Three checks, each verified to FAIL against PR #17's actual diff before being committed: config.ts exports no *TEMPO* constant; stepLivePlay's dt argument is the bare identifier `delta` (scoped to that call -- the replay's FX.REPLAY.SPEED playback clock legitimately scales delta and never reaches the sim); and getPitchBaseMs's body contains no arithmetic at all, checked structurally rather than by variable name.
simClock.notABan: A tempo dial is a legitimate product decision -- lib.js's own header says TEMPO is 'the single absolute dial and is a product decision, not a measurement'. What this forbids is adding one INVISIBLY. Teach the conformance records to derive the tempo instead of hardcoding 1, then delete the lint in the same commit, with the reasoning attached.

sim.note: The v2 SIM's constants. A new reference class: these answer to PUBLISHED PHYSICS and to real baseball, not to BB2001 footage -- which is why every record carries `reference`, and why that field became required in the same change. Conforming a game for four-to-eight-year-olds to MLB's strikeout rate is the mistake that field exists to prevent.

ballPhysics.what: The ball and the air it flies through, folded into the single factor the aerodynamic model needs: K = 1/2 * rho * A / m.
ballPhysics.why: K is the validation, not just a convenience. It combines air density, cross-sectional area and mass, so deriving it from the four published constants and comparing against Nathan's INDEPENDENTLY published figure exercises all three at once. That is a better check than terminal velocity, which the plan originally called for: terminal velocity is only ever as good as the C_D you assume, and C_D is the least certain input here.
ballPhysics.theGap: 0.29%, and it is NATHAN'S ROUNDING rather than our arithmetic. His Eq. 9 normalises on 'the density of air is nominally 1.225 kg/m^3 (or 0.0767 lb/ft^3)', but 1.225 kg/m^3 is really 0.076482 lb/ft^3. Feeding his rounded 0.0767 into our own formula reproduces 5.509e-3 exactly, which is what proves the difference is bookkeeping. Recorded rather than reconciled: adopting a rounded density to make two numbers agree is fitting the constant to the citation.
ballPhysics.nNote: n=1 is the right number for a published constant. This is a rulebook and a standard atmosphere, not a sample.
ballPhysics.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts 'derives K from the published constants and lands on Nathan figure', which also reproduces his value from his own rounded density.

aeroModel.what: Drag and Magnus lift, taken verbatim from Nathan's Trajectory Calculator fit rather than invented.
aeroModel.model: C_D = C_D0 + C_D1*(omega/1000rpm), with C_D0 0.297 and C_D1 0.0292. C_L = C_L2*S/(C_L0 + C_L1*S), with C_L0 0.583, C_L1 2.333, C_L2 1.120, and S = R*omega/v.
aeroModel.theHappyConsequence: BOTH FORMS ARE PURE ARITHMETIC. The plan assumed the coefficients would need committed interpolation tables, because ECMAScript specifies Math.exp/log/pow and the trig functions as implementation-approximated while only + - * / and Math.sqrt are correctly rounded -- so a determinism fingerprint built on them goes red on a V8 bump and reads as somebody's bug. Nathan's fit needs none of them. The whole aerodynamic model is bit-stable with no tables at all, and purity.lint.test.js now enforces that the per-step path stays that way.

validation.conditions: 100 mph exit velocity, 30 deg launch angle, 3 ft contact height.
validation.against: The Statcast rule of thumb that a well-struck ball (100mph/30deg) carries about 400 ft. Backspin must also carry FURTHER than no spin and topspin SHORTER, asserted separately.

aeroModel.caveat: THE FIT IS NOT FOR OUR REGIME, and that is recorded rather than glossed. It comes from MLB fly balls with exit velocity >= 90 mph and launch angles 20-35 deg, measured indoors at Tropicana Field (Nathan estimates rho = 1.194 there), and he verifies C_D's velocity-independence only 'at least for speeds in the range 60-110 mph'. Our batters hit 35-50 mph. Everything below 60 mph is an unvalidated extrapolation. The model is conformed on what was published; the extrapolation is not, and sim.aeroModelLowSpeed is where that gets closed.
aeroModel.nNote: n=1 for a published fit: the sample is Nathan's, not ours.
aeroModel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts -- the coefficient forms, the saturating C_L bound, drag's independence from speed, and the MLB carry band.

aeroModelLowSpeed.what: Whether Nathan's drag fit still holds at the 35-60 mph exit velocities a four-to-eight-year-old actually produces.
aeroModelLowSpeed.why: His stated result is that after accounting for spin there is 'no further dependence on v, at least for speeds in the range 60-110 mph'. Every ball this game cares most about is below that band. The model may well hold -- Reynolds number falls with speed and the drag crisis is at the other end -- but nobody has said so, and the point of this file is that unmeasured things stay enumerable instead of becoming folklore.

ours.value: Nathan's fit, extrapolated below its verified band.

aeroModelLowSpeed.whatWouldWork: Either a published low-speed C_D measurement for a real baseball (Kensrud & Smith, 'In situ drag measurements of sports balls', Procedia Engineering 13 (2011), covers a wider speed range and is the first place to look), or a direct one: launch a ball at a measured speed and angle with known spin, film it against a scale, and fit C_D from the trajectory. n>=3 per speed bin.

integratorStep.what: What FLIGHT_HZ is actually for, measured rather than inherited from the design doc.
integratorStep.theFinding: NOT ACCURACY. docs/OVERVIEW.md promised 'integrated RK4 at 240Hz' before any integrator existed, and the natural assumption is that 240 was an accuracy figure. It is not: RK4 here is fourth order (measured error ratios 16.20 and 16.13 per halving of the step, against a textbook 2^4 = 16), and ACCURACY IS SATURATED BY 60 Hz -- a 60 Hz flight lands within 3e-9 ft of a 15360 Hz one, and 240 Hz within 6e-12 ft. Nothing in this game can see 3e-9 ft.
integratorStep.whatItIsFor: Two things, both real. (1) PHASE: 240 = 4x60 = 2x120, so at both common refresh rates the fixed-timestep accumulator's remainder is exactly zero and the renderer's interpolation alpha is exact. (2) COLLISION SAMPLING: guards are evaluated once per step, so the step size bounds how briefly a condition can hold and still be noticed. Bisection makes a DETECTED crossing exact; it cannot detect one that opens and closes inside a single step.

measured.method: The same launch integrated at each rate; error is the carry difference against a 15360 Hz reference.

integratorStep.theTestTrap: The first version of the convergence test compared 240/480/960 Hz and got a ratio of ZERO, which read as a broken integrator. At those rates the discretisation error is already at the double-precision floor, so the ratio was measuring rounding. A convergence test has to run COARSE to measure convergence -- the same class of error as pace.pitchCorridor's 'the tolerance was the noise'.
integratorStep.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/flight.test.ts -- fourth-order convergence on a clean flight AND through a bounce (the second is what catches an event handler that bisects and then Euler-steps the remainder, which every clean-flight test passes while the global order silently drops to one), plus the phase divisibility.

carryVsFence.what: How much exit velocity it takes to clear each venue's fence, against how hard a four-to-eight-year-old can actually hit a ball.
carryVsFence.why: This was the v2 plan's ranked #1 risk, written as 'every ball is a home run' -- MLB-shaped exit velocities over a 200ft park. The truth is the MIRROR IMAGE, and the integrator alone was enough to find it, before any contact model, fielder or play reducer existed that could have absorbed a wrong answer by being tuned around it.

measured.conditions: 1500 rpm backspin, 2.5 ft contact height, optimal launch angle swept 10-50 deg.

carryVsFence.theProblem: Published youth guidance puts 8-and-under exit velocity at 45-55 mph off a TEE, with game exit velocity 5-10 mph lower -- so a real 4-8-year-old hits 35-50 mph and clears NOTHING. The park's shortest fence needs 57.5 mph and its centre field needs 62.5.

drift.note: Between the top of a realistic kid's game exit velocity (50) and the park's easiest fence (57.5).

carryVsFence.resolution: DECIDED, and it is a game-design decision rather than a physics one: THE POWER STAT EARNS IT. The fences stay. PR 4 maps power 1-10 onto roughly 35-60 mph exit velocity, so only genuine sluggers clear the short parts, the park's 212ft centre stays out of reach for everyone, and the sandlot's 150ft porch becomes the cheap-homer park its own data file already intends. That costs no geometry change, makes `power` legible on the field, and makes the draft matter -- which is the product.
carryVsFence.whyNotShrinkTheFences: It was the obvious alternative and it loses more than it gains: pulling the fences to 140-165ft means pulling FIELD_POSITIONS in with them to keep the fence-to-outfield-depth ratio near MLB's 1.25, which drops the outfield to about 2 basepaths. A deep outfield a gap ball can land in is the entire reason v2 exists -- v1 had 1.49 basepaths and 0% BABIP.

ours.value: park 185/212, sandlot 150-207, blacktop 188 -- unchanged by this PR.

carryVsFence.whatWouldClose: PR 4's power-to-exit-velocity mapping, then re-running this table against the roster's actual power distribution: the record should end up asserting that a power-10 kid clears the park's line and a power-5 kid does not.

flyHangRatio.what: Kid-scale fly-ball hang time as a RATIO to the home-to-first anchor -- the one place real RK4 physics can be checked against a measurement this project made itself.
flyHangRatio.why: Absolute hang times cannot be compared across two games with different field scales, which is why pace.flyHang recorded a ratio in the first place. That makes it the only BB2001 measurement transferring to v2 unchanged: no pixels, no new capture, and it checks EMERGENT physics rather than a constant somebody typed.
flyHangRatio.verdict: Kid-scale flies land at the LOW end of BB's measured band, and the shallowest fall below it. That is the expected direction -- a 45 mph pop-up cannot hang like a 95 mph one -- and the deep flies that matter for defensive play (EV 55-60) sit inside it. Recorded as conformed on the deep-fly cases with the shallow ones stated, rather than claiming the whole range.
flyHangRatio.nNote: The BB band's n=4 and low confidence are inherited from pace.flyHang; this record cannot be more confident than the anchor it is measured against.

bounceModel.what: The FORM of a ground impact: normal restitution, plus a tangential grip/slip branch that couples the ball's spin to its forward speed.
bounceModel.model: Normal: vy' = -e*vy. Tangential: the contact point's horizontal velocity is u = v_t + w x (-R*yhat). Gripping it costs an impulse of (2/7)*m*|u|; Coulomb friction can supply mu*m*(1+e)*|vy|. If it can afford it the contact point stops (GRIP), giving v' = (5v - 2wR)/7; otherwise the full friction impulse is applied opposing the slip (SLIP). Spin updates from the same impulse in both branches.
bounceModel.whyConformed: The form is DERIVABLE, and was derived rather than recalled: solving the impulse problem for a sphere (I = 2/5 mR^2, contact one radius below the centre) with the rolling-contact condition gives J = -(2/7)m(v + wR) directly. Verified three ways in bounce.test.ts -- pure rolling in gives zero impulse, an unspun ball gives exactly 5/7, and angular momentum about the contact point is conserved in BOTH branches, which is the property the 2/7 is a consequence of rather than an assumption alongside.
bounceModel.theSign: v' = (5v - 2wR)/7. The MINUS is the part memory gets wrong, and getting it wrong makes backspin behave like topspin. Its consequence is checked directly: forward speed falls monotonically with backspin, is roughly halved at a realistic 200 rad/s (1910 rpm), and reverses only between 300 and 800 rad/s -- 2900 to 7600 rpm, off the top of the real batted-ball range. The headline 'backspin bounces the ball BACKWARD' is true of the model and NOT true of a baseball, and the record says so rather than repeating the catchier version.
bounceModel.emergentAndCorrect: TOPSPIN ACCELERATES THE BALL off the bounce -- measured here at 12.21 -> 12.92 ft/s -- because friction converts rotational energy into translational. Total energy still falls (191.7 -> 111.9). The first version of the test asserted that speed never increases, failed on exactly this case, and looked like a bug when it was the physics being right. The invariant is ENERGY, and the acceleration is now asserted directly so nobody re-caps it.
bounceModel.knownSimplification: Cross (2002) measured that real balls GRIP rather than roll, with the friction force reversing mid-bounce and the spin exceeding the rolling prediction. Our grip branch is the idealised limit, so it under-predicts spin reversal. Sidespin-induced lateral deflection is also unmodelled: the impulse is applied in the plane of the slip, and spin about the vertical is left untouched.
bounceModel.nNote: n=1 for a derivation. It is checked by conserved quantities, not by sampling.
bounceModel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/bounce.test.ts 'the ground bounce' -- contact point at rest after a grip, exactly 5/7 unspun, rolling-in-stays-rolling, angular momentum conserved across both branches, slip when the impact is too glancing, and energy never increasing on a full sweep of every venue.

groundBounce.what: The ground coefficient of restitution for each venue's surface -- the COEFFICIENT, where sim.bounceModel is the form.

partialReading.source: Brosnan & McNitt's Pennbounce work at Penn State's Center for Sports Surface Research.
partialReading.theCheckItAlreadyBuys: At COR_BASE 0.50 the venue multipliers that were hand-authored MONTHS BEFORE this band was found land at park 0.50 and sandlot 0.40 -- both inside it -- while the blacktop's 0.65 falls outside, correctly, because asphalt is not a turf surface and the band is for infields. A cross-check of somebody else's guesswork against real literature, and it held.
partialReading.why: Read from a secondary summary of the primary papers rather than the papers themselves, and the band covers infield surfaces rather than the mown outfield grass, shaggy backyard lawn and asphalt this game actually has. n=1 source, not n=1 measurement.

groundBounce.whatWouldWork: Read Brosnan & McNitt directly for the per-surface figures; or measure it, which is genuinely cheap: drop a baseball from a measured height onto mown grass, shaggy grass and asphalt, film against a scale, and take COR = sqrt(rebound height / drop height). n>=3 per surface.

rollFriction.what: The rolling friction coefficient per surface, which sets how far a grounder travels once it stops bouncing.
rollFriction.why: field.ts authors 0.28 (mown grass), 0.36 (shaggy backyard grass) and 0.10 (asphalt) with a comment and no citation. They are now load-bearing: a ball rolling at v covers exactly v^2/(2*mu*g), so mu IS the roll distance.
rollFriction.whatWouldWork: Roll a baseball from a measured initial speed across each surface and time it to a stop, then invert the closed form: mu = v^2 / (2*g*d). A phone camera and a tape measure are enough. n>=3 per surface. The ORDERING is not in doubt (asphalt < mown grass < shaggy grass); the magnitudes are.

wallRestitution.what: The coefficient of restitution off each venue's outfield wall, and how much tangential speed a carom keeps.
wallRestitution.why: A ball off the wall is a double, so this decides how often the deepest hits pay. The Pennbounce band does NOT apply -- it is for GROUND surfaces, and a painted wall, wooden planks and chain-link are three different problems.
wallRestitution.whatWouldWork: Throw a ball at a measured speed square into each wall type and film the rebound; COR is the speed ratio. The tangential figure needs an oblique throw and two angles measured. n>=3 each. Chain-link is the interesting one -- it is a net, not a wall, and may not behave like a restitution at all.

venueRollFeel.what: Which venue plays FAST, once bounce and roll are both simulated -- and the answer contradicts what the venues were authored to be.
venueRollFeel.theFinding: THE BLACKTOP PLAYS SHORTEST. It has by far the lowest rolling friction (0.10 against 0.28 and 0.36), and in isolation a ball rolling on it travels 3.6x as far. But end to end a batted ball comes to rest SHORTEST there, because its restitution is also the highest (0.65): the ball spends its energy BOUNCING rather than rolling -- 6 or 7 hops against 3 or 4 -- and every landing takes tangential speed out through the grip. A surface cannot be both the springiest and the fastest.

measured.conditions: EV 70mph, launch angle 8 deg, spray -20, 1200 rpm, contact 2.5ft.
measured.isolatedRollRatio: asphalt rolls 3.6x as far as shaggy grass from the same entry speed -- the friction model is doing exactly what it should.

drift.note: The sandlot's shaggy grass -- the surface authored to be the DEADEST -- carries a ball nearly twice as far as the asphalt authored to be the fastest.

venueRollFeel.theIntent: data/venues.ts calls the blacktop 'hot asphalt -- the ball SPRINGS' and gives it rollMult 1.3, i.e. the fast park; the sandlot gets 'dead hops off the lumpy lawn'. v1 could hold both because its bounceMult and rollMult were independent renderer-domain knobs with no physics between them. Real physics couples them.
venueRollFeel.whyNotJustRetune: Because that would be tuning a constant to make a test pass, which is the failure mode this whole file exists to catch. The blacktop's high restitution is the CORRECT reading of a hard surface -- Pennbounce found COR tracks surface hardness directly. What is wrong is the expectation that hard also means fast.
venueRollFeel.whatWouldClose: A venue-feel pass in the retune PR, with the choice made explicitly: either accept that the blacktop is a high-hop park and change its description, or lower bounceMult and accept a less springy asphalt. Both are legitimate; picking one quietly is not.
venueRollFeel.pinnedBy: src/v2/sim/bounce.test.ts 'plays SHORTEST on the blacktop', which pins the drift ratio between 1.5 and 2.5 so it can neither grow nor be half-fixed unnoticed.

defense.note: Constants governing the CPU defense. SCALED 1.987x with RUNNER_SPEED in the 2026-07-24 retune but STILL NOT MEASURED -- they are the values most likely to need feel iteration, because halving runner speed doubles the time the defense has and the scaling assumes BB's defense is slow in the same proportion its runners are. If the retune plays wrong, start here. As of 2026-07-28 the first of them HAS been retuned: see fielderSpeed, which was the one constant in this block that had no record at all.

fielderSpeed.what: How fast a fielder runs, expressed against the pace anchor: fielders and baserunners are THE SAME KIDS, so the honest ratio is 1.0. A kid does not get faster by putting a glove on.
fielderSpeed.comparisonForm: fielder speed / runner speed -- both px/s in the same space, so the ratio is dimensionless and survives BB being 640x480 while we are 960x640. Reads as plain English: 'a fielder runs N times as fast as a baserunner.' Sanity band: 0.9x-1.4x. Outside that, one of the two is wrong -- and it sat at 2.48x through every retune of the constant it is measured against.
fielderSpeed.whatWouldWork: THIS ONE IS ACTUALLY MEASURABLE, unlike its neighbours in this block. defense.throwSpeed and defense.cpuThrowDelay are blocked on tracking a ~5px ball; a RUNNING FIELDER is a big sprite crossing open grass, the same target class as the runner in pace.homeToFirst (which reached n=3). Method: pick a fielder breaking for a ball on a capture that passes video.js clockFidelity, read first-motion and arrival frames magnified >=2x (flags=neighbor -- at 1x a pose change reads as motion, the exact trap that produced the withdrawn 270ms pitch corridor), convert px/s against the same basepath scale pace.homeToFirst used, and divide by 48.17px/s. n>=3 before promoting: the repo's own n<3 rule exists because overclaiming is how the 270 happened.
fielderSpeed.invariant: cpuFielderSpeedMult MUST equal playerRunSpeedMult in every mode. That is what holds the ratio on the side the human BATS, and its absence is what let kid mode drift to its own separate value (0.62) that happened to compensate for a base that was 2.48x too high.
fielderSpeed.retuneNote: FIELDER_SPEED 106 -> 42.8 px/s (ratio 2.48x -> 1.0x) and MODES.kid.live.cpuFielderSpeedMult 0.62 -> 1.3. Kid mode's ABSOLUTE CPU fielder speed barely moved (65.7 -> 55.6): it was the one branch already near 1.0x, because the 0.62 was silently cancelling most of the bad base. DERIVED, not measured -- this record claims nothing about BB.
fielderSpeed.history: The most useful thing in this record. FIELDER_SPEED sat at 210 px/s through FIVE consecutive runner slowdowns -- 280fe50 175 (1.20x), 67b9d87 150 (1.40x), 164cd55 117 (1.79x), 96f320e 106 (1.98x), 7a859ca 85 (2.47x) -- and the 2026-07-24 retune (4b93867) then scaled BOTH by 1/1.987, faithfully preserving 2.48x. Every time the defense could not get outs the fix was 'slow the runners', never 'check the fielder'. Two commit titles say it outright: 'Rebalance the fielding race: throwing runners out is finally possible' and 'Backyard-pace the fielding race: slower runners and ball, snappier throws'. Nothing caught it because this was the ONLY pace constant with no record here and no pin in conformance.test.js -- every neighbour had both. The lesson is not 'someone typed a wrong number'; it is that an ungoverned constant absorbs the error of every governed one around it.
fielderSpeed.symptom: An outfielder could charge into the infield, field the ball, and still beat the batter to first -- carry speed equals chase speed with no penalty (liveplay.ts moveFielders), so running the ball in was a viable defensive play. At 106px/s a center fielder carried it to the plate (268px) in 2.5s against a 4.2s basepath leg. The slowest possible fielder (84.8px/s) outran the fastest possible baserunner (55.6px/s) by 1.5x.
fielderSpeed.exposed: Slower fielders surfaced TWO latent bugs that faster ones had been hiding. (1) Doubling a runner off a caught fly ONLY ever worked via the carrier footracing them for a tag -- the CPU's throw path was gated behind cpuThrowDelayMs + CATCH_GATHER_MS (1192 + 1100 = 2292ms), which no throw-behind can beat. Fixed in liveplay.ts catchGatherFor: the gather beat is about runners ADVANCING (it is what makes a sac fly a real race) and does not apply to a throw behind a runner scrambling back. (2) The maxPlayMs straggler settle read `r.from`, but reverseLeg SWAPS from/to -- so a runner turned back from the plate carries from === 4 while running toward third, having never touched home. They settled standing ON home with no run scored, and finishLivePlay writes bases[3] on a 3-element tuple, so the runner silently vanished from the inning. Fixed to settle on min(from, to), clamped 1-3. Longer plays (slower fielders reach maxPlayMs far more often) are what made a latent edge case reachable; the random send/hold property test caught it only stochastically, so it is now pinned deterministically at the seam.
fielderSpeed.notSufficient: THIS DOES NOT MAKE BASE HITS POSSIBLE, and saying so here is the point of the record. Measured against the real sim after the change (CLASSIC, human batting, CPU fielding, stat-5 batter, 4197ms leg): routine grounder to SS out by 1397ms, slow roller to 3B out by 347ms, ball through the 5-6 hole out by 1047ms, TRUE LF-CF gap out by 897ms, TRUE CF-RF gap out by 1097ms, down the RF line out by 2047ms. Every ball a fielder reaches is still a putout at first. What the ratio fix DID close is the specific pathology it was aimed at: the carry. A center fielder ran the ball to the plate in 2.53s and to first in 1.94s, against a 4.2s leg; those are now 6.26s and 4.81s, so running it in is dead, and at 42.8px/s a fielder can no longer outrun a grounder (GROUNDER_SPEED 81-121px/s) and must intercept instead.
fielderSpeed.nextLever: defense.throwSpeed, NOT this record. The binding term on a batter-to-first race is the fixed overhead plus the throw, not the chase: cpuReactionMs 835 + cpuThrowDelayMs 1192 = 2027ms of standing still (48% of the whole leg), then a ~480ms throw. The dimensionless tell is in defense.throwSpeed.comparisonForm: CLASSIC throws at 9.65x runner speed where KID -- the mode that actually produces base hits -- throws at 4.60x (413 x 0.62 = 256 vs its 55.64px/s runner). Two modes sitting at 9.65x and 4.60x inside a 3x-20x sanity band is exactly the kind of internal inconsistency that band exists to surface.
fielderSpeed.structuralNote: A deeper reason no single speed constant separates hits from outs: our outfield is too shallow relative to the diamond. CF sits 268px from home against a 179.6px basepath -- a 1.5x ratio, where real baseball is ~3.3x. So an outfielder's throw is barely longer than an infielder's (SS->1B 229px vs CF->1B 206px -- the OUTFIELDER's is SHORTER), and throw distance cannot discriminate. Down the RF line is out by 2047ms, FASTER than the routine grounder to short, because 1B is standing right there. Any real fix to offense has to touch geometry.FIELD_POSITIONS or the throw ratio, not the chase.

cpuReaction.what: Delay between contact and the fielding team actually breaking for the ball.

partialReading.method: Background-subtracted fielder tracks (kids are ~20x35 native, so the size filter that cannot isolate a 5px ball works cleanly on them), decimated to distinct frames, linked with lib.js linkTracks. Reaction = first frame the biggest-moving infielder has left its start by >6px and stays gone. Grounders specifically: on a FLY the chaser often does not move at all, because BB paints the landing disc where the ball will go and the nearest fielder is frequently already standing on it -- fly plays gave 817-3283ms of noise for exactly that reason.
partialReading.why: NOT promoted, for two reasons that are about the measurement rather than the spread. (1) DEFINITIONAL: a displacement threshold cannot separate a DECISION DELAY from an ACCELERATION RAMP. Our cpuReactionMs is a deliberate AI pause; if BB's fielders instead start immediately and accelerate slowly, the same 1050ms would be measuring something we do not model, and scaling our constant to it would be wrong. An eye read of play-15 shows a fielder genuinely STATIC for ~0.67s and then breaking, which favours a real delay -- but that is n=1 and not enough to settle it. (2) IDENTIFICATION: without ball tracking the PRIMARY fielder cannot be picked out reliably, and 'biggest mover' also selects kids who are backing up or covering a base, which is different behaviour with its own timing.
partialReading.whatWouldResolveIt: Per-play eye reads on grounders: watch the fielder who actually gathers the ball, and check whether he holds a standing pose for a beat (decision delay) or shifts into a run pose immediately and covers ground slowly (acceleration ramp). BB's pose set makes that visible -- it is the same read that settled the fly hang. Roughly one sheet per play across the five grounders.

cpuReaction.ifItHolds: Taken at face value the partial reading is ~2.5x our 420ms, which is the same direction and rough size as every other measured pace drift (run 0.50x, between-pitch 0.49x). That consistency is suggestive, and it is NOT evidence -- three separate clean-looking numbers were wrong this session before being looked at.

poseEvidence.finding: play-15, 33ms sheet from the cut: the fielding kid holds a STANDING pose for ~0.67s and only then shifts to a run pose and covers ground.
poseEvidence.implication: That favours a real DECISION DELAY -- something comparable to our cpuReactionMs -- rather than a pure acceleration ramp, which is the confound that keeps this record from being promoted.
poseEvidence.why: n=1 is not enough to promote. One fielder on one play could be hesitating for a reason specific to that play (the ball was hit elsewhere, he is not the primary). The read is cheap and repeatable though: the same 33ms sheet on plays 03/04/12/17 would settle it, and the partialReading's five samples are already waiting for that verdict.

cpuThrowDelay.what: How long a CPU fielder holds the ball before releasing a throw.

blocked.finding: Needs the BALL: the beat is 'fielder gathers it' -> 'ball separates and accelerates away'. Ball tracking in the wide view is the open problem recorded in instrument.background-subtraction and pace.flyHang -- the fly hang was measured off the landing DISC precisely because the ball itself is not reliably trackable there.
blocked.whatWouldWork: The gather and release are both visible as POSE changes on a large sprite (glove-down, then throw). Reading those by eye sidesteps ball tracking entirely, and is the same technique that would settle defense.cpuReaction. Not reached.

blocked.whatWouldWork: The infield-throw family: a fielder gathers a grounder and throws to 1B, whose native coordinates are exact (473.7, 311.2). throwSpeed.comparisonForm: throw speed / runner speed -- both px/s in the same space, so the ratio is dimensionless and survives BB being 640x480 while we are 960x640. Reads as plain English: 'a throw travels N times as fast as a kid runs.' OURS = THROW_SPEED_MAX 413 x cpuThrowSpeedMult 1.0 / (RUNNER_SPEED 42.8 x playerRunSpeedMult 1.0) = 9.65x (player charge range 277-413 gives 6.5-9.65x). BB = measured px/s / (202.3px / 4.200s = 48.17px/s). Sanity band: a throw must land between 3x and 20x a run; outside that the read is wrong. NOTE (corrected 2026-07-28): this string quoted the PRE-RETUNE 820 and 85 until then. The ratio it concludes was coincidentally unaffected (820/85 = 413/42.8 = 9.65x), so no test went red, but the absolute numbers contradicted ours.max two lines below. Prose is not asserted; keep derived figures out of it where you can, and stamp them where you can't.

chaserElection.what: WHICH fielder chases a loose ball is now a decision with its own constants, not a fixed consequence of geometry. Recorded because the two obvious metrics both fail, and both failures are cheap to rediscover and expensive to diagnose.
chaserElection.finding: Ranking candidates by 'who can reach the ball soonest' hands essentially every grounder to the PITCHER. A grounder starts at HOME and rolls outward, so P -- 112px from the plate -- is nearest its early path at every spray angle, and wins the race to cut it off before anyone else is close. Adding a distance-to-settle penalty term does not separate them (swept lambda 0..8 ms/px, no crossover). Gating candidacy on the SETTLE point instead does: the pitcher is simply not a candidate for a ball that comes to rest 122px+ from the mound, which is what a real defense does. But that alone is still not enough -- a third baseman can genuinely reach a ball rolling AT the shortstop 125-257ms sooner by charging across in front of him. True on the clock, wrong on a ball field. So the ball belongs to whoever's zone it settles in, and a challenger must beat that fielder by CUT_AHEAD_MS.

measuredWindow.how: Cut-off times computed against the real predictLoosePath and the real fielder speeds for four reference launches (grounder settling at the shortstop's feet at two roll speeds, the shallow-right grounder that motivated the work, and a comebacker). Below 257 the third-baseman-poaches-shortstop case returns; above 523 the second baseman stops cutting off the shallow-right grounder and it dribbles through to the outfielder.
measuredWindow.stabilityClaimCorrected: 2026-07-28. This block used to end 'Stable across both kid and main fielder speeds.' That held over the range it was tested at -- kid 65.7px/s vs main 106px/s, a 1.6x spread -- and is NOT a general claim. CUT_AHEAD_MS is a fixed ms gate compared (fielding.ts electChaser: `c.ms + CUT_AHEAD_MS >= ownerMs`) against BALL-PATH times returned by cutOff(). Slowing fielders pushes every interception later along the path, so the gaps between candidates inflate while the gate does not -- it gets relatively cheaper to clear and the zone owner is overridden more often. It cannot be speed-neutral by construction.
measuredWindow.measuredDrift: Swept a 20px grid of grounder settle points x 4 roll speeds (n=1372), counting how often electChaser returns someone other than the fielder whose POST is nearest the settle point: at 106px/s + 400ms the owner is overridden 27.7% of the time; at 42.8px/s + 400ms, 32.4%. A 4.7-point drift -- real, and far smaller than a first-principles estimate suggests, which is why it was measured rather than assumed.
measuredWindow.whyNotRetunedAt42_8: Restoring 27.7% needs CUT_AHEAD_MS ~600 (measured: 600 -> 26.5%), which is ABOVE this record's own upperBound of 523 -- past which the second baseman stops cutting off the shallow-right grounder. But that bound was itself derived at 106px/s and moves with the speed too, so 600 is not knowably safe, only knowably outside a stale window. BOTH bounds must be re-derived at 42.8px/s against the same four reference launches before this constant moves. Left at 400 deliberately: a measured 4.7-point drift is not worth trading for an unmeasured bound violation.

chaserElection.why: BB2001 was NOT measured for this. The election is tuned against baseball sense and our own geometry, not against a capture -- the same standing caveat as the rest of the defense block. It also makes the CPU defense meaningfully better on grounders (it cuts balls off instead of trailing them), so it is a live candidate for the first feel-tuning pass. Lower CUTOFF_GRACE_MS first (fewer cut-offs), then the corner/middle leashes -- not cpuFielderSpeedMult, which is on the scaled pace path and would desynchronise it.

fieldingAssist.what: How much CLASSIC's magnet assist steers the player's fielder toward the ball, now scaled per difficulty tier rather than one flat constant.
fieldingAssist.why: Recorded because the flat 0.5 blend was not a mild helper -- it was the whole play. Measured against the real sim: steering PERPENDICULAR to a fly for its entire hang time still left the fielder 5.3px from the landing spot, well inside the 39px catch reach. The game caught the ball for you no matter where you pointed, so defense had no skill in it. At the tiered blends the same deliberate mis-steer ends 102px off on MEDIUM and 189px off on HARD -- both clean misses.
invariants: The magnet lerps between two candidate points each within one movement step, so it can only REDIRECT, never add speed. A liveplay test pins the per-tick cap at every tier.

assistIdleSpeedMult must stay < 1 at every tier. The idle amble is only fair while it is worse than steering, and that is a RELATIVE claim -- weakening the magnet without also slowing the amble would have made doing nothing the optimal defense on HARD. That is why the hard tier scales its idle knobs alongside its magnet.
fieldingAssist.whatWouldWork: BB2001's assist strength has no on-screen representation -- nothing renders it, so no frame can be read for it, exactly like the swing windows (see pace.swingWindows). It could only be inferred behaviourally: drive BB's fielder along a fixed WRONG heading through a fly's full hang time on a known field, and measure how far the sprite drifts from its own steering line toward the landing spot. That needs frame-accurate input injection into the emulator, which this instrument does not have. Until then these are feel dials, tuned by playing -- not conformance targets.
